---
title: next.config.js
description: Learn how to configure your application with next.config.js.
url: "https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js"
docs_index: /docs/llms.txt
version: 16.3.0
lastUpdated: 2025-11-04
prerequisites:
  - "API Reference: /docs/app/api-reference"
  - "Configuration: /docs/app/api-reference/config"
---


> For an index of all Next.js documentation, see [/docs/llms.txt](/docs/llms.txt).
Next.js can be configured through a `next.config.js` file in the root of your project directory (for example, by `package.json`) with a default export.

```js filename="next.config.js"
// @ts-check

/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  /* config options here */
}

module.exports = nextConfig
```

## ECMAScript Modules

`next.config.js` is a regular Node.js module, not a JSON file. It gets used by the Next.js server and build phases, and it's not included in the browser build.

If you need [ECMAScript modules](https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html), you can use `next.config.mjs`:

```js filename="next.config.mjs"
// @ts-check

/**
 * @type {import('next').NextConfig}
 */
const nextConfig = {
  /* config options here */
}

export default nextConfig
```

> **Good to know**: `next.config` with the `.cjs` or `.cts` extensions are currently **not** supported.

## Configuration as a Function

You can also use a function:

```js filename="next.config.mjs"
// @ts-check

export default (phase, { defaultConfig }) => {
  /**
   * @type {import('next').NextConfig}
   */
  const nextConfig = {
    /* config options here */
  }
  return nextConfig
}
```

### Async Configuration

Since Next.js 12.1.0, you can use an async function:

```js filename="next.config.js"
// @ts-check

module.exports = async (phase, { defaultConfig }) => {
  /**
   * @type {import('next').NextConfig}
   */
  const nextConfig = {
    /* config options here */
  }
  return nextConfig
}
```

### Phase

`phase` is the current context in which the configuration is loaded. You can see the [available phases](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/5e6b008b561caf2710ab7be63320a3d549474a5b/packages/next/shared/lib/constants.ts#L19-L23). Phases can be imported from `next/constants`:

```js filename="next.config.js"
// @ts-check

const { PHASE_DEVELOPMENT_SERVER } = require('next/constants')

module.exports = (phase, { defaultConfig }) => {
  if (phase === PHASE_DEVELOPMENT_SERVER) {
    return {
      /* development only config options here */
    }
  }

  return {
    /* config options for all phases except development here */
  }
}
```

## TypeScript

If you are using TypeScript in your project, you can use `next.config.ts` to use TypeScript in your configuration:

```ts filename="next.config.ts"
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  /* config options here */
}

export default nextConfig
```

The commented lines are the place where you can put the configs allowed by `next.config.js`, which are [defined in this file](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/server/config-shared.ts).

However, none of the configs are required, and it's not necessary to understand what each config does. Instead, search for the features you need to enable or modify in this section and they will show you what to do.

> Avoid using new JavaScript features not available in your target Node.js version. `next.config.js` will not be parsed by Webpack or Babel.

This page documents all the available configuration options:

## Unit Testing (experimental)

Starting in Next.js 15.1, the `next/experimental/testing/server` package contains utilities to help unit test `next.config.js` files.

The `unstable_getResponseFromNextConfig` function runs the [`headers`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/headers), [`redirects`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/redirects), and [`rewrites`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/rewrites) functions from `next.config.js` with the provided request information and returns `NextResponse` with the results of the routing.

> The response from `unstable_getResponseFromNextConfig` only considers `next.config.js` fields and does not consider proxy or filesystem routes, so the result in production may be different than the unit test.

```js
import {
  getRedirectUrl,
  unstable_getResponseFromNextConfig,
} from 'next/experimental/testing/server'

const response = await unstable_getResponseFromNextConfig({
  url: 'https://nextjs.org/test',
  nextConfig: {
    async redirects() {
      return [{ source: '/test', destination: '/test2', permanent: false }]
    },
  },
})
expect(response.status).toEqual(307)
expect(getRedirectUrl(response)).toEqual('https://nextjs.org/test2')
```

  - Use `allowedDevOrigins` to configure additional origins that can request the dev server.
- [appDir](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/appDir)

  - Learn to add and access environment variables in your Next.js application at build time.

  - Next.js will generate etags for every page by default. Learn more about how to disable etag generation here.

  - Add custom HTTP headers to your Next.js app.

  - Specify a list of user agents that should receive blocking metadata.

  - Next.js will automatically use HTTP Keep-Alive by default. Learn more about how to disable HTTP Keep-Alive here.

  - Custom configuration for the next/image loader

  - Configure the Next.js cache used for storing and revalidating data to use any external service like Redis, Memcached, or others.

  - Enable inline CSS support.

## Unit Testing (experimental)

Starting in Next.js 15.1, the `next/experimental/testing/server` package contains utilities to help unit test `next.config.js` files.

The `unstable_getResponseFromNextConfig` function runs the [`headers`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/headers), [`redirects`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/redirects), and [`rewrites`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/rewrites) functions from `next.config.js` with the provided request information and returns `NextResponse` with the results of the routing.

00022| import { dirname } from 'node:path';

00030|  *     structured JSON event stream we parse for the transcript).
00031|  *   - `--model <model>` is appended when a model override is present.
00032|  *   - else, when modelPolicy === 'native-default', `--print-logs --log-level INFO`
00033|  *     is appended so older OpenCode versions print the CLI-selected model (the
00034|  *     log-scrape path) without a follow-up export call.
00035|  *
00036|  * @param {{prompt:string, model?:string, modelPolicy?:string}} input
00037|  * @returns {string[]}
00038|  */

00052|  * Preserved verbatim from the old adapter.
00053|  *
00054|  * @param {string|undefined|null} output
00055|  * @returns {string|undefined}
00056|  */

00063|   // Filter to only include lines that look like JSON objects.
00064|   const lines = output.split('\n').filter((line) => {

00081|  * @param {string} output
00082|  * @returns {string|undefined}
00083|  */
00084| export function extractObservedModelFromOpenCodeOutput(output) {

00092|     const providerMatch = line.match(/providerID=([^\s]+)/);

00095|     const modelID = modelMatch?.[1];
00096|     if (providerID && modelID) {

00098|     }

00101|   return observedModel;
00102| }

00106|  * Every emitted event carries a `sessionID` field.
00107|  * Preserved verbatim from the old adapter.
00108|  *
00109|  * @param {string|undefined} transcript
00110|  * @returns {string|undefined}
00111|  */

00113|   if (!transcript) {
00114|     return undefined;
00115|   }

00117|   for (const line of transcript.split('\n')) {

00119|       const event = JSON.parse(line);
00120|       if (typeof event.sessionID === 'string' && event.sessionID) {
00121|         return event.sessionID;
00122|       }

00125|     }
00126|   }
00127| 
00128|   return undefined;
00129| }
00130| 
00131| /**
00132|  * Extract the observed model from `opencode export <sessionID>` output.
00133|  * Assistant messages carry `providerID` and `modelID` in their info.
00134|  * Preserved verbatim from the old adapter.
00135|  *
00136|  * @param {string} exportOutput
00137|  * @returns {string|undefined}
00138|  */
00139| export function extractObservedModelFromSessionExport(exportOutput) {
00140|   const start = exportOutput.indexOf('{');
00141|   if (start === -1) {
00142|     return undefined;
00143|   }
00144| 
00145|   let parsed;
00146|   try {
00147|     parsed = JSON.parse(exportOutput.slice(start));
00148|   } catch {
00149|     return undefined;
00150|   }
00151| 
00152|   const messages = parsed.messages;
00153|   if (!Array.isArray(messages)) {
00154|     return undefined;
00155|   }
00156| 
00157|   for (const message of messages) {
00158|     const info = message.info;
00159|     if (info?.role !== 'assistant') {
00160|       continue;
00161|     }
00162|     if (
00163|       typeof info.providerID === 'string' && info.providerID &&
00164|       typeof info.modelID === 'string' && info.modelID
00165|     ) {
00166|       return `${info.providerID}/${info.modelID}`;
00167|     }
00168|   }
00169| 
00170|   return undefined;
00171| }
00172| 
00173| /**
00174|  * Run OpenCode over the workspace at `input.cwd` and return a RunnerResult.
00175|  *
00176|  * Auth (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and OPENCODE_ENABLE_EXA when web research is on)
00177|  * arrives via process.env — the orchestrator sets it on the `node run.mjs`
00178|  * invocation, and we pass process.env straight through to the CLI. The runner
00179|  * never handles secrets itself.
00180|  *
00181|  * @param {import('../plugin/contract.js').AgentRunInput} input
00182|  * @returns {Promise<import('../plugin/contract.js').RunnerResult>}
00183|  */
00184| export async function runAgent(input) {
00185|   const args = buildOpenCodeCliArgs(input);
00186| 
00187|   // spawnSync (not a shell string): the prompt is a plain argv element, so there
00188|   // is no shell quoting/escaping to get wrong. Blocking is fine — the runner has
00189|   // nothing else to do while the agent works. The sandbox-level timeout bounds it.
00190|   const res = spawnSync('opencode', args, {
00191|     cwd: input.cwd,
00192|     env: process.env,
00193|     encoding: 'utf8',
00194|     maxBuffer: 64 * 1024 * 1024,
00195|   });
00196| 
00197|   const stdout = res.stdout || '';
00198|   const stderr = res.stderr || '';
00199|   // Preserve the old concatenation order: stdout THEN stderr.
00200|   const output = stdout + stderr;
00201|   // spawnSync sets status=null + error when the binary can't be spawned at all.
00202|   const agentExitCode = res.status == null ? -1 : res.status;
00203| 
00204|   // Capture the transcript from the combined output (old: over stdout+stderr).
00205|   const transcript = extractTranscriptFromOutput(output) ?? null;
00206| 
00207|   // Resolve the model OpenCode actually used. The `--format json` events never
00208|   // include it, so first try scraping the printed logs (works on OpenCode <=
00209|   // 1.16.x), then fall back to `opencode export <sessionID>`, whose assistant
00210|   // messages carry providerID/modelID (OpenCode 1.17.0 changed the log format,
00211|   // which broke the scrape). Observation must never fail the run.
00212|   let observedModel = extractObservedModelFromOpenCodeOutput(output);
00213|   if (!observedModel) {
00214|     const sessionId = extractSessionIdFromTranscript(transcript ?? undefined);
00215|     if (sessionId) {
00216|       try {
00217|         const exportRes = spawnSync('opencode', ['export', sessionId], {
00218|           cwd: input.cwd,
00219|           env: process.env,
00220|           encoding: 'utf8',
00221|           maxBuffer: 64 * 1024 * 1024,
00222|         });
00223|         if ((exportRes.status == null ? -1 : exportRes.status) === 0) {
00224|           observedModel = extractObservedModelFromSessionExport(exportRes.stdout || '');
00225|         }
00226|       } catch {
00227|         // Leave observedModel undefined.
00228|       }
00229|     }
00230|   }
00231|   const observedModelOrNull = observedModel ?? null;
00232| 
00233|   if (res.error || agentExitCode !== 0) {
00234|     // Mirror the old error string: last 5 lines of output, else a coded fallback.
00235|     const errorLines = output.trim().split('\n').slice(-5).join('\n');
00236|     const fallback = res.error
00237|       ? `Failed to run opencode: ${res.error.message}`
00238|       : `OpenCode CLI exited with code ${agentExitCode}`;
00239|     return {
00240|       ok: false,
00241|       output,
00242|       transcript,
00243|       observedModel: observedModelOrNull,
00244|       error: errorLines || fallback,
00245|       agentExitCode,
00246|     };
00247|   }
00248| 
00249|   return {
00250|     ok: true,
00251|     output,
00252|     transcript,
00253|     observedModel: observedModelOrNull,
00254|     error: null,
00255|     agentExitCode,
00256|   };
00257| }
00258| 
00259| /* ─────────────────────────── runnable (CLI) entry ─────────────────────────── */
00260| 
00261| // True when this file is executed directly (`node run.mjs ...`), false when imported.
00262| const isMain = process.argv[1] && fileURLToPath(import.meta.url) === process.argv[1];
00263| 
00264| if (isMain) {
00265|   // argv[2] is the AgentRunInput JSON (never contains secrets).
00266|   const input = JSON.parse(process.argv[2]);
00267| 
00268|   // Always produce a RunnerResult, even if the runner itself throws, so the host
00269|   // always has a result file to read (node exit code stays 0 except on a truly
00270|   // unrecoverable crash before we can write).
00271|   let result;
00272|   try {
00273|     result = await runAgent(input);
00274|   } catch (e) {
00275|     result = {
00276|       ok: false,
00277|       output: '',
00278|       transcript: null,
00279|       observedModel: null,
00280|       error: e && e.message ? e.message : String(e),
00281|       agentExitCode: -1,
00282|     };
00283|   }
00284| 
00285|   // Source of truth: the result file the host reads back via sandbox.readFile.
00286|   try {
00287|     mkdirSync(dirname(input.resultPath), { recursive: true });
00288|     writeFileSync(input.resultPath, JSON.stringify(result));
00289|   } catch {
00290|     // If the file can't be written, the host falls back to the marker line below.
00291|   }
00292| 
00293|   // Fallback channel: a compact status line (no transcript — it can be huge).
00294|   process.stdout.write(
00295|     '__AGENT_RESULT__ ' +
00296|       JSON.stringify({
00297|         ok: result.ok,
00298|         observedModel: result.observedModel,
00299|         error: result.error,
00300|         agentExitCode: result.agentExitCode,
00301|       }) +
00302|       '\n'
00303|   );
00304| 
00305|   // Exit 0: "the runner ran". Agent success/failure is conveyed via result.ok, not
00306|   // the node exit code (the host distinguishes the two).
00307|   process.exit(0);
00308| }
00309| 

(End of file - total 309 lines)
</file>

One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 00008| 00009| Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 00010| 00011| React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 00012| 00013| This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 00014| 00015| ## Add view transitions with an agent 00016| 00017| The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app. 00018| 00019| Install the skill: 00020| 00021| ```bash filename="Terminal" 00022| npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-view-transitions 00023| ``` 00024| 00025| Then prompt the agent with something like: 00026| 00027| ```prompt 00028| Add view transitions to this app using the vercel-react-view-transitions skill. 00029| ``` 00030| 00031| Or prompt for a specific transition, such as: 00032| 00033| - ---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Add view transitions with an agent

The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app.

Install the skill:

---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Add view transitions with an agent

The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app.

Install the skill:

events.content:
View transitions are in place:

- **Shared element morph** — thumbnail and hero share `product-${slug}` so the image morphs between grid and detail
- **Directional slides** — `nav-forward` / `nav-back` on links; pages slide left going in, right going back
- **Suspense reveals** — skeleton exits down, content enters up
- **Reduced motion** — all view-transition durations are `0s` when `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` is set
